In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/vma: call ->may_split() before a partial merge

A driver can use the ->may_split() hook to forbid a VMA boundary at
certain addresses.

A device-dax device is a character device that gives raw access to a
range of memory through mmap(). device-dax refuses any address that is not
a multiple of the device's alignment through vm_ops->may_split.

vma_merge_existing_range() can move boundaries, but does not call
vm_ops->may_split.

If a range at the edge of a VMA gets the attributes of the adjacent VMA,
the function moves only that range over to the neighbour: one VMA shrinks
and the other grows. This is a partial merge, and vma_modify() tries it
before any split.

Take a device-dax VMA that lies next to another VMA of the same file.
The user calls mprotect() on the one page of the first VMA that touches
the second VMA, and asks for the protection that the second VMA already
has. The result is a partial merge. It puts the boundary inside a 1 GiB
mapping, which is a single leaf entry at the PUD level.

As part of the merge, the kernel looks for a huge PMD to split at the
new boundary. That code does not expect a PUD leaf:

    vma_merge_existing_range()
      commit_merge()
        vma_adjust_trans_huge()
          split_huge_pmd_address()
            mm_find_pmd()
              treats the PUD leaf as a pointer to a PMD table,
              so the "table" is the device memory that the leaf maps
            __split_huge_pmd()
              reads a PMD that the user wrote to the device memory
              folio_put() on the folio that this PMD names

Bad. While the code must at some point be taught to split PUD entries as
well, the issue here is that we move VMA boundaries such that they are
incompatible with the driver.

Fix this by calling ->may_split() on the address that a partial merge
would move the boundary to, and by abandoning the merge if the driver
refuses. vma_modify() then tries the split, which fails with -EINVAL.

Factor out existing split handling into check_split() and reuse it.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: improve description; cleanup the code ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/huge_memory: split huge PUDs when adjusting VMA boundaries

PFN mappings such as VFIO PCI BAR mappings can use PUD leaves while
allowing VMA splits at page granularity. However, vma_adjust_trans_huge()
only handles PMDs.

After faulting a writable PUD-sized VFIO BAR mapping, changing its first
page to read-only with mprotect() makes the PMD walk treat the PUD leaf
as a PMD table. Applying MADV_DONTFORK to the first PMD-sized chunk leaves
the PUD spanning two VMAs: the PMD-aligned boundary skips splitting.

Walk the page tables once at each adjusted boundary and split a huge
PUD or PMD leaf as needed. Handle PUD leaves even when the boundary is
PMD-aligned.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/vma: don't leak the charge for stack growth

acct_stack_growth() charges stack expansion even without VM_ACCOUNT.
This can happen for read-only or MAP_NORESERVE mappings created with
MAP_GROWSDOWN. Unmapping these VMAs does not release the charge, leaking
Committed_AS.

Only check and charge growth for VM_ACCOUNT VMAs, matching mremap().
Unaccounted growth skips the overcommit check while remaining subject
to the other stack-growth limits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/cma: don't release CMA pages still in use

When a driver calls dma_free_contiguous() before quiescing DMA, the
page might still have a reference from the device.
put_page_testzero() there returns false, WARN fires, but the code proceeds
to free_contig_frozen_range() putting a live page onto buddy and clearing
the bitmap. A subsequent allocation can hand the same PFN to a new
owner while the original holder still references it.

A concurrent put_page() that drops the last reference between the
testzero loop and free_contig_frozen_range() can double-queue the page
via page->lru, corrupting buddy lists.

Avoid the corruption by not freeing a CMA region if any of the
pages inside are still in use.

Make it explicit in the warning that the driver allowed a leak.

While at it, use page_ref_freeze() to make the semantics clearer and
switch to pr_warn_ratelimited().

[ david: use page_ref_freeze() + pr_warn_ratelimited() ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/memory-tiers: unregister empty tiers outside memory_tier_lock

When offlining a node's last memory empties its tier,
clear_node_memory_tier() calls device_unregister() while holding
memory_tier_lock. A concurrent sysfs read can hold a kernfs active
reference and block in nodelist_show() on that mutex. device_unregister()
then waits in kernfs_drain() for the read to finish and release its active
reference, while the reader waits for the offlining task to release the
mutex.

Return the node's former tier from clear_node_memory_tier(), making the
helper more similar to set_node_memory_tier(), which also returns a
memory_tier pointer. Let the caller unlink an empty tier under
memory_tier_lock before rebuilding demotion targets, then unregister its
device after dropping the lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

khugepaged: fix readahead lock inversion in collapse_file()

collapse_file() can call page_cache_sync_readahead() while still holding
source folios locked. If truncate holds mapping->invalidate_lock
exclusively and waits for one of those folios, readahead waits for
invalidate_lock and neither side can make progress.

We need to release those folio locks before starting readahead. On a page
cache miss, roll back first, populate the collapse range, and retry once.
Doing readahead after rollback avoids an extra pass when all folios are
already present. If another miss occurs on retry, give up rather than keep
retrying while truncate or reclaim removes folios.

Keep page_cache_sync_readahead() and wait for read I/O with
filemap_lock_folio(), releasing each folio before moving to the next. The
existing uptodate check during collapse still handles read errors.

Shmem uses shmem_get_folio() for swapin and fallocated folios without
taking mapping->invalidate_lock, so it is unaffected.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/gup: check folio->mapping under folio lock in memfd_pin_folios()

memfd_pin_folios() pins folios from the page cache without taking the
folio lock. khugepaged or MADV_COLLAPSE can therefore replace a folio
after checking its refcount while memfd_pin_folios() still pins the old
folio. The caller then receives a folio which is no longer part of the
memfd.

For udmabuf and iommufd, this can cause data corruption: DMA accesses
the detached folio rather than the live memfd contents. DMA reads can
return stale data, while DMA writes update the detached copy and are
lost from the live memfd. The detached folio remains pinned, so these
accesses do not constitute a use-after-free or target another
application's memory. For memfd live update, the stale contents can
reappear in the memfd after handover.

Lock the folio and recheck folio->mapping before pinning it, like other
page cache users do. If the folio was removed, retry the folio lookup
from the index that was removed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: fail the mount if the casefold flag has changed

An unprivileged user in a user namespace can repeatedly trigger a kernel
warning with their own overlay mounts. They do so by changing the
casefold flag of the topmost layer's empty root, the top directory of
that layer, after the layers are set and before the mount is created.

The casefold flag of a directory makes name lookups in that directory
case-insensitive. All layers of an overlay must agree on casefolding.

ovl_mount_dir_check() reads the casefold flag of a layer root when
fsconfig() sets that layer, and saves the result in ofs->casefold. The
mount is created later, by another fsconfig() call with
FSCONFIG_CMD_CREATE.

The casefold flag of an empty directory can be changed.

The casefold flag of the overlay root must match ofs->casefold.
ovl_get_root() copies the flag from the topmost layer root, as it is
when the mount is created. On a mismatch, ovl_get_root() only does a
WARN_ON(), and the mount continues. The check is not a WARN_ON_ONCE(),
so each such mount warns again.

An unprivileged user needs CONFIG_UNICODE, and a tmpfs mounted with the
casefold option in their namespace.

Reproduced by changing the casefold flag of the empty upper directory
after the layers were set and before FSCONFIG_CMD_CREATE, with tmpfs and
ext4 layers, and as uid 1000 in a user namespace.

Fix this by replacing the WARN_ON() with a check that fails the mount
with -EINVAL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: do not let chattr change the casefold flag

chattr +F or -F on an overlay directory can make the directory, or the
whole mount, unusable. Lookups of the directory, and lookups in it, then
fail. From code inspection, the caller only needs to own the directory.
The upper filesystem must support casefolding: ext4 or f2fs with the
casefold feature, or tmpfs with the casefold option.

chattr +F and -F set and clear FS_CASEFOLD_FL, the casefold flag of a
directory. The flag enables casefolding (case-insensitive name lookup)
for the directory. All directories of an overlay must match the casefold
state that was recorded at mount time, and ovl_lookup_single() enforces
this:

- A lookup in a directory that does not match fails with -ESTALE.
- A lookup of the directory itself fails with -EREMOTE.

ovl_fileattr_set() copies the directory up, which creates it in the
upper layer if it only existed in a lower layer. It then passes
FS_CASEFOLD_FL on to the upper filesystem. The upper filesystem accepts
the change if the upper directory is empty, regardless of what the
merged directory contains. The merged directory is the one that the user
sees, with the names from the upper and the lower directories.

After the change the upper directory no longer matches the mount. If the
directory is the root of the overlay, the whole mount is affected.

The flag can also change without chattr +F or -F. chattr reads all flags
of a directory, changes one and writes all of them back. For a directory
that only exists in a lower layer, overlayfs reads the flags from the
lower filesystem. xfs with the ascii-ci feature reports FS_CASEFOLD_FL
on every inode, but never sets S_CASEFOLD, the inode flag that overlayfs
compares with the mount. So its directories count as not casefolded.
With a lower layer on such an xfs and an upper layer on ext4 with the
casefold feature, chattr +A on a lower-only directory therefore sets
FS_CASEFOLD_FL on the new, empty upper directory.

Reproduced as root on tmpfs and on ext4 with chattr +F or -F on an
overlay directory whose upper directory was empty. Afterwards lookups
below it failed with ESTALE, and lookups of the directory itself failed
with EREMOTE. The chattr +A case was seen once, on a kernel with an
earlier form of this patch that still passed the caller's flag on:
lookups of the directory failed with EREMOTE.

Fix this by returning -EOPNOTSUPP if FS_IOC_SETFLAGS, the only call that
can change the flag, asks for a casefold flag on a directory that does
not agree with the casefold state of the mount. This also refuses the
chattr +A case above.

[amir: check the flag against the casefold state of the mount instead of
 reading back the flags]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: fix whiteout creation in casefolded directories

unlink and rmdir fail with EINVAL on an overlay with casefolded
(case-insensitive) layers, if the name exists in a lower layer.
Casefolded layers need CONFIG_UNICODE. Root can mount such an overlay,
and so can an unprivileged user in a user namespace, with tmpfs layers.

Overlayfs does not change a lower layer. To remove a name that exists
there, it hides the name with a marker file, a whiteout. It creates the
whiteout in the work directory, a scratch directory on the upper
filesystem, and renames it over the name in the upper directory:

- ovl_whiteout() creates the whiteout with mknod, or as a hard link to
  an earlier whiteout.
- ovl_cleanup_and_whiteout() then prepares the rename with
  start_renaming_two_dentries(), which returns -EINVAL if the source or
  the target dentry is unhashed, that is, not in the dentry hash table.

With casefolded directories, both dentries can be unhashed:

- The target. Lookup in a casefolded directory leaves a negative dentry
  unhashed, so the rename target is unhashed if the name does not exist
  in the upper directory.
- The source, which is the new whiteout. tmpfs hashes a dentry when
  mknod or link makes it positive, but ext4 does not, so on ext4 the
  source is unhashed as well.

The cleanup after the failure also refuses an unhashed dentry, so on
ext4 the whiteout is left behind in the work directory.

Reproduced with rm and rmdir on casefolded tmpfs and ext4 layers, also
as uid 1000 in a user namespace.

Fix this by creating the whiteout with ovl_create_temp(), which repeats
the lookup if the new dentry is unhashed. Prepare the rename with
start_renaming_dentry(), which looks up the target name with the
directories locked. The caller looked the name up without a lock, so
return -ESTALE if the name now refers to a different inode.

[amir: pass the name used for lookup instead of taking a name snapshot]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: clamp skb->queue_mapping before indexing the tx queue

This issue was caught by Sashiko (nipa). A producer-side path cap is
already merged (ea4d4b5dddb5); this patch adds the matching consumer-side
caps.

The issue:
The tx queue is picked and capped in netdev_core_pick_tx() before the
__dev_xmit_skb() qdisc enqueue path. A tc BPF program running inside an
egress qdisc (not clsact) can then change __sk_buff->queue_mapping; that
store is never re-checked. bpf_convert_ctx_access() bounds it only by
NO_QUEUE_MAPPING, not by the device's queue count.

Two consumers read the stale value:

  - On dequeue, qdisc_restart() calls netdev_get_tx_queue(), which
    indexes dev->_tx[]. netdev_get_tx_queue() guards it with just a
    DEBUG_NET_WARN_ON_ONCE, so sch_direct_xmit() takes the out-of-bounds
    txq->_xmit_lock and writes txq->xmit_lock_owner past the end of the
    allocation on non-lltx devices such as ifb. Drivers that index their
    rings from skb_get_queue_mapping() (ex: ifb) go out of range the same
    way.

  - On enqueue, taprio_enqueue() indexes q->qdiscs[] with the same value;
    the array is sized dev->num_tx_queues. A duplicating netem on a child
    qdisc clones the skb and re-enqueues the clone at the taprio root
    (qdisc_root_bh()) through a direct rootq->enqueue() call, so the value
    reaches taprio_enqueue() before any dequeue cap runs.

The Fix:
Cap the mapping at the consumers and write the capped value back, so the
qdisc's _tx[] lookup, the taprio q->qdiscs[] lookup and any later driver
read stay in range.

On the dequeue side the cap folds into the dequeue path instead of a
separate walk over the returned list: dequeue_skb() caps the head, and
each bulk helper caps the element it appends. For a qdisc that is not
TCQ_F_ONETXQUEUE, netdev_cap_txqueue() logs a ratelimited notice and
selects queue 0.

A TCQ_F_ONETXQUEUE qdisc is bound to a single tx queue: dequeue_skb() uses
q->dev_queue for the frozen check, the BQL limit and the trace point, while
qdisc_restart() transmits on the skb's queue. Capping an out-of-range
mapping to queue 0 would therefore send a per-queue child's skb through a
different queue than the one it was dequeued for. On mq, mqprio, taprio and
htb offload children, a stopped queue 0 could then park the list in
q->gso_skb, and the later wake would schedule queue 0's own child instead
of this qdisc. Pin a TCQ_F_ONETXQUEUE mapping to the qdisc's own queue to
keep the documented invariant.

The pin covers every mapping, not only an out-of-range one: an in-range
mapping that a filter sets on one of those per-queue children is rewritten
to the child's own queue, and this path does not call netdev_cap_txqueue(),
so it logs no notice. On a single-queue device qdisc_create() sets
TCQ_F_ONETXQUEUE, so the one-queue trigger described below also takes this
branch and is corrected without a notice.

That also keeps a bulk list on one queue by construction: every element of
a TCQ_F_ONETXQUEUE qdisc, including a follower changed by a filter, is
pinned to q->dev_queue before it is appended. The fast bulk helper
therefore needs no head comparison and no skb_bad_txq requeue; the slow
helper, used only by non-ONETXQUEUE qdiscs, still compares and requeues a
mismatched follower, where a wake on any queue reschedules q.

On the enqueue side taprio_enqueue() caps the mapping against
real_num_tx_queues and writes it back before selecting q->qdiscs[queue], so
a duplicating child cannot steer the clone out of the array.

Conditions to recreate the bug:
The dequeue path: load a SCHED_CLS or SCHED_ACT program that stores
__sk_buff->queue_mapping (a tc BPF action is enough), attach it to a
transmit qdisc (for example a matchall filter on a prio root), and send a
packet. With a 1-queue device a store of 1 indexes one past dev->_tx[].
Under KASAN with panic_on_warn=1 the unfixed kernel faults with "BUG:
KASAN: slab-out-
---truncated---

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: inherit FMODE_NONOTIFY when opening directory realfiles

When fanotify hands a listener an fd for a permission event on an
overlay directory, ovl_dir_open_realfile() opens the real directory via
dentry_open(), not backing_file_open(), so the lower open could still
raise FS_OPEN_PERM and deadlock a listener that also marks the backing
filesystem.

Export dentry_open_nonotify() and call it from ovl_path_open_realfile()
when the overlay user file must not generate events.  Ordinary
ovl_path_open() callers are unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: reject a negative TCP header offset in qdisc_pkt_len_segs_init()

qdisc_pkt_len_segs_init() stores skb_transport_offset(), or the inner
offset, in the unsigned hdr_len. A header in front of skb->data gives a
negative offset. For an offset a little below zero, pskb_may_pull() gets a
small length and succeeds. Then a 64-bit kernel reads the TCP header far
after the skb and can crash. Further below zero pskb_may_pull() fails.

Commit 28a57fb2c5df ("net: iptunnel: fix stale transport header during
tunnel decapsulation") fixed one source of such offsets. Other code that
removes bytes from the front of a packet can leave the same stale header.

Return SKB_DROP_REASON_SKB_BAD_GSO for a negative offset in the TCP branch.
SKB_GSO_UDP_L4 and the other GSO types read no header and still get a wrong
qdisc_pkt_len(). On a 64-bit kernel only packets that cause the read after
the skb today get a new result. Then __dev_queue_xmit() drops them and
returns -EINVAL, but sch_handle_ingress() ignores the result. Their content
can be valid. Thus the code that leaves the header stale needs its own fix.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost/vsock: size receive SKBs from declared payload

vhost_vsock_alloc_skb() sizes the skb from iov_length(), the total guest
descriptor length.  virtio_transport_inc_rx_pkt() instead adds hdr->len to
rx_bytes and buf_used, and budgets each queued skb as SKB_TRUESIZE(0).  The
guest controls the descriptor length and hdr->len independently.

A guest can therefore provide a 64 KiB descriptor while declaring a zero
payload.  The descriptor-sized skb remains queued, rx_bytes and buf_used
remain unchanged, and only the fixed queue-entry budget limits retention.
This is not a lifetime leak: the skb is freed when dequeued or at socket
teardown.  Repeating this across connections can nevertheless exhaust host
memory.  On Linux v7.2, 455 such descriptors retained 30,255,680 bytes for
a 262,144-byte receive buffer; a full-payload control retained 265,984
bytes.

Vhost previously read hdr->len and allocated pkt->buf from that value.  The
conversion from virtio_vsock_pkt to sk_buff instead allocated receive skbs
from the descriptor length, introducing the allocation-accounting mismatch.

Copy the header into a stack object and validate hdr->len before allocating
the skb.  Size the allocation as sizeof(hdr) + payload_len so descriptor
capacity no longer determines queued memory.  Check payload_len against
len - sizeof(hdr) to avoid addition overflow on 32-bit hosts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mptcp: do not use Fast Open on MP_JOIN subflows

tcp_fastopen_create_child() hands the SYN packet itself to
subflow_syn_recv_sock(). For an MP_JOIN request this takes the
fatal fallback: the cloned child is destroyed and handed back with
drop_req flagged, but tcp_fastopen_create_child() does not check
the flag and queues it, so accept() can expose the freed child.

MP_JOIN cannot use Fast Open: data on a subflow requires the
completed HMAC exchange (RFC 8684, sec. 3.2). Refuse it (only the
TFO path passes a SYN skb here) and let tcp_conn_request() fall
back to the regular MP_JOIN handshake; also strip the Fast Open
cookie from MP_JOIN SYN/ACKs.

[ Moving code to avoid clearing TS and consolidating checks. ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: keep the CS user fence BO in GTT

The CS ioctl hands the GPU the GART address of the user fence BO, but
since the BO keeps its own preferred and allowed domains, it no longer
makes sure the BO is in GTT. A user fence in a VRAM BO, which only needs
to be a page in size, gets its address from amdgpu_bo_gpu_offset(), which
warns about non-contiguous VRAM. On navi31, a CS with a user fence in a
4K VRAM BO, or in one created with AMDGPU_GEM_CREATE_VM_ALWAYS_VALID:

  WARNING: amdgpu_object.c:1531 at amdgpu_bo_gpu_offset+0x86/0xb0 [amdgpu], CPU#11: cs_gem_checks/18393
  RIP: 0010:amdgpu_bo_gpu_offset+0x86/0xb0 [amdgpu]
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   amdgpu_cs_parser_bos.isra.0+0x4eb/0x850 [amdgpu]
   amdgpu_cs_ioctl+0x97e/0x2510 [amdgpu]
   drm_ioctl_kernel+0xac/0x110 [drm]
   drm_ioctl+0x2c6/0x5b0 [drm]
   __x64_sys_ioctl+0xa0/0xf0
   do_syscall_64+0xa3/0x4d0
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x76/0x7e

and BOs which can't be in GTT at all, like GWS or OA ones of a page in
size, pass the checks as well.

Only take BOs which can't be anywhere else than in GTT as user fence,
which the CS then validates there along with its other BOs. While at it,
detect userptrs with amdgpu_ttm_tt_is_userptr(); amdgpu_ttm_tt_get_usermm()
returns NULL once the task which created the userptr is gone.

v2: only take BOs which can only be in GTT instead of special casing the
    user fence BO in the validation, use amdgpu_ttm_tt_is_userptr()
    (Christian)

(cherry picked from commit f16989def9561d04d0f2e77216f5319112d29bf1)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdkfd: use the queue's process info for the WPTR BO eviction fence

amdgpu_amdkfd_map_gtt_bo_to_gart() removes the eviction fence of
bo->vm_bo->vm->process_info from the WPTR BO of a new queue. bo->vm_bo
is the VM which opened the BO last, not necessarily the KFD process' VM,
and a render node VM has no process info.

On navi31, an unprivileged process which exports its WPTR BO with
AMDKFD_IOC_EXPORT_DMABUF and imports it on a second render node fd
oopses in AMDKFD_IOC_CREATE_QUEUE:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000060
  RIP: 0010:amdgpu_amdkfd_map_gtt_bo_to_gart+0x86/0x1a0 [amdgpu]
   init_user_queue.part.0+0x180/0x250 [amdgpu]
   pqm_create_queue+0x32d/0x730 [amdgpu]
   kfd_ioctl_create_queue+0x583/0x9f0 [amdgpu]

Pass the process info of the queue instead. With the fix, the queue is
created and destroyed normally.

(cherry picked from commit 6b4157498a176bd1c6083f6bb5aaf8a257a2027e)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: check amdgpu_vm_ready() in dma-buf move notify

amdgpu_dma_buf_move_notify() touches the page tables without first
calling amdgpu_vm_ready(). When a process is SIGKILLed, its VM entities
are stopped. Teardown of an imported dma-buf then tries to clear PTEs by
submitting to one of those stopped entities. That eventually hangs the
task.

Commit aa5fc4362fac ("drm/amdgpu: fix task hang from failed job
submission during process kill") added the stopped entity check in
amdgpu_vm_ready() and used it in amdgpu_cs_vm_handling(). That did not
cover a call in amdgpu_dma_buf_move_notify(), what was already mentioned
in:
https://lists.freedesktop.org/archives/amd-gfx/2025-October/133076.html

Tested by SIGKILLing a GPU workload holding imported dma-bufs. Without
the patch "Trying to push to a killed entity" errors are logged, then a
task hangs. With the patch there are no hung tasks. This was tested on a
6.18 kernel.

(cherry picked from commit bee5c9d7a34cb1b510ad3b4c18c30f9d38b0ab7d)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu/userq: validate the moved individual BOs on restore

An individual BO of a user queue VM, i.e. one which doesn't share the
root reservation, goes to the individual needs_update list when it is
evicted. The user queue restore looked at vm->invalidated for them, which
the VM state machine rework turned into the always_valid evicted list and
commit 18decfc9e8cc ("drm/amdgpu/userq: actually validate userq BOs")
into the individual evicted one. That list only holds imported DMA-bufs of
compute VMs though, so for a user queue VM nothing is validated.

The restore then neither locks such a BO nor moves it back. Its PTEs are
updated to wherever it is now, cleared if it went to system memory, and
it doesn't get the new eviction fence, so it can move again under the
running queue.

On navi48, once the BOs of an SDMA user queue are evicted from GTT
(debugfs amdgpu_evict_gtt) the queue faults on its ring and rptr:

  amdgpu 0000:03:00.0:   in page starting at address 0x0000000100000000 from client 10
  amdgpu 0000:03:00.0: 	 Faulty UTCL2 client ID: SDMA0 (0xd)
  amdgpu 0000:03:00.0:   in page starting at address 0x0000000100101000 from client 10

Validate the BOs on the individual needs_update list like before.

(cherry picked from commit eb0d94765d4be18d41e93ad09947dd9cc06ed31a)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: clear RB_OVERFLOW bit when enabling interrupts for navi10_ih

Port this change to navi10_ih.c:
commit afbf7955ff01 ("drm/amdgpu: clear RB_OVERFLOW bit when enabling interrupts")

Setting IH_RB_WPTR to 0 does not clear RB_OVERFLOW if RB_ENABLE is not
set. Pulse WPTR_OVERFLOW_CLEAR after RB_ENABLE (and with
WPTR_OVERFLOW_ENABLE) so overflow is cleared when interrupts are
enabled.

(cherry picked from commit 713fb4ab04f4d2af6120f8eb607c5673b2759b38)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amd/display: Avoid closing unowned DDC pins

[WHY]
dal_ddc_open() cleans up pins it acquires on later failures. If the

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

arm64: mm: validate /dev/mem mmap ranges without overflow

An arm64 syzkaller reproducer creates a FUSE character device with
major:minor 1:1, so opening it uses the /dev/mem file operations. It
maps one page from offset 0xfffffffffffff000 at user address zero.
The next openat() with a NULL pathname triggers a synchronous external
abort (SEA, ESR 0x96000010) in strncpy_from_user() via do_getname(),
panicking the kernel.

valid_mmap_phys_addr_range() checks the exclusive end by adding the
mapping size to the starting address. For this offset, the sum wraps
to zero and passes the PHYS_MASK test, allowing an out-of-range PFN to
reach remap_pfn_range(). The inclusive-end overflow check in
mmap_mem_prepare() does not catch it because the end is ULONG_MAX.

Reject starting PFNs outside PHYS_MASK and compare the inclusive length
against the remaining physical range without overflowing. This also
allows mappings that end exactly at PHYS_MASK, which the old check
incorrectly rejects.

[catalin.marinas@arm.com: changed the check to look more like __access_ok()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: look up the index by the decoded origin

A file opened by file handle on an overlay with nfs_export=on can show
the stale lower data of a file that was copied up to the upper layer.
While the file opened this way stays in the inode cache, a lookup of the
copied up file by path fails with ESTALE for all users. The open can
also succeed for a file that was removed, where it has to fail with
ESTALE. This happens with a handle that has one byte changed. The handle
comes from an NFS client, or from a process that calls
open_by_handle_at() with CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH in the initial user
namespace.

When a file in a lower layer is about to be modified, overlayfs first
copies it to the upper layer (copy up). With nfs_export=on, each copy up
also creates an entry in the index directory, a directory that overlayfs
keeps for itself on the upper filesystem.

The handle of an overlay file that comes from a lower layer wraps the
handle of its lower inode. Overlayfs calls this lower inode the origin.
The overlay handle stays valid after a copy up.

To decode such a handle, ovl_lower_fh_to_d() first decodes the wrapped
handle to the origin. If no overlay inode is cached for the origin, it
looks in the index directory:

- An index entry there leads to the upper file.
- A whiteout, the marker that overlayfs uses for a removed file, means
  that the overlay file was removed.

The name of an index entry is the handle that copy up encoded for the
origin, as a hex string.

ovl_lower_fh_to_d() builds the name for this lookup from the bytes that
the caller passed in. But handles with different bytes can decode to the
same inode:

- Overlayfs ignores some flag bits of the handle.
- A lower filesystem can accept a different fid type, extra bytes, or
  generation 0 for any generation.

Such a handle decodes to the origin but misses the index entry or the
whiteout. So the decode returns an overlay inode that has only the lower
file.

While that inode is cached, a path lookup of a copied up file fails with
ESTALE, since the upper file that the lookup finds does not match the
cached inode, which has none.

Reproduced on tmpfs and on ext4 with open_by_handle_at(), after a copy
up and a mount cycle. A handle in which one flag bit, the fid type, the
length or the generation was changed read the old lower data, and path
lookups returned ESTALE.

Fix this by re-encoding the decoded origin and building the index name
from that handle.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

l2tp: only return sessions of the given tunnel in l2tp_session_get()

Commit 5f77c18ea556 ("l2tp: use IDR for all session lookups") made
pppol2tp_connect() and the netlink session commands find sessions with
l2tp_session_get(), passing the socket of the tunnel they name.

L2TPv3 session IDs are unique per network namespace, except that
sessions carried over UDP are only unique per UDP socket, the socket of
their tunnel. However, l2tp_v3_session_get() only checks the socket when
another session has the same session ID. Otherwise it returns the
session, whichever tunnel it belongs to. As of now, a session command
that names the wrong tunnel acts on a session of another tunnel, and a
PPPoL2TP socket for a second L2TPv3 tunnel fails with EEXIST, because it
finds session 0 of the first tunnel.

The issue can be reproduced with:

    ip l2tp add tunnel tunnel_id 3 peer_tunnel_id 3 encap udp \
        local 127.0.0.1 remote 127.0.0.1 udp_sport 5003 udp_dport 6003
    ip l2tp add tunnel tunnel_id 4 peer_tunnel_id 4 encap udp \
        local 127.0.0.1 remote 127.0.0.1 udp_sport 5004 udp_dport 6004
    ip l2tp add session tunnel_id 3 session_id 7 peer_session_id 7
    ip l2tp del session tunnel_id 4 session_id 7
    ip l2tp show session

Before that commit, the delete fails with "No such device", and session
7 of tunnel 3 is still listed. After that commit, the delete succeeds,
and session 7 of tunnel 3 is gone.

This patch will make l2tp_session_get() return NULL when the L2TPv3
session it finds does not belong to the given socket. The receive path
calls l2tp_v3_session_get() directly and is not changed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/nouveau/nvkm: clear use.enabled when subdev init fails

On Kepler boards without the video decode falcon firmware installed
(msvld/mspdec/msppp), every other VA-API decode attempt binds to an
engine with no ucode loaded. The submitted work never completes, which
leads to a context switch timeout, a channel recovery that cannot reset
the engine, and eviction waits on fences that never signal. The process
ends up stuck in D state, or killed by SIGBUS when it touches a buffer
evicted after the wait times out:

  msvld: unable to load firmware data
  msvld: init failed, -19
  fifo: SCHED_ERROR 0a [CTXSW_TIMEOUT]
  vo[5444]: channel 14 killed!
  WARNING: drivers/gpu/drm/nouveau/nvkm/engine/fifo/runl.c:117 at nvkm_runl_rc+0x2a4/0x3b0 [nouveau]
  [TTM] Buffer eviction failed
  WARNING: drivers/gpu/drm/nouveau/nouveau_bo.c:1092 at nouveau_bo_move_ntfy.part.0+0x9b/0x100 [nouveau]

Tracing nvkm_subdev_ref() and nvkm_subdev_init_() shows the pattern:
a reference taken with enabled=0 runs nvkm_falcon_init(), which
returns -ENODEV; the next reference sees enabled=1 and succeeds
without running it.

Clear use.enabled when init() fails, so that every later reference
retries init and fails cleanly.  The other readers of use.enabled are
fini() handlers that use it to skip teardown, which they now also do
after a failed init().

On a GK107 (Quadro K1100M) without video firmware, playing H.264 with
mpv --hwdec=auto: without this patch the GPU channel is killed within a
minute and mpv hangs; with it, VA-API decoder creation fails, mpv falls
back to software decoding, and no faults are logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: cs46xx: Handle SCB creation failures before dereferencing

With CONFIG_PM_SLEEP enabled, cs46xx_dsp_create_scb() can return NULL
if kmemdup() fails to allocate the SCB data saved for resume.
cs46xx_dsp_scb_and_task_init() and _dsp_create_generic_scb() dereference

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: hda/tas2781: Only accept CRC-less V1 data if all entries are valid

Commit 408249089c48 ("ALSA: hda/tas2781: Accept V1 calibration data
without CRC") only checked the first device entry. On machines where
the BIOS populates fewer entries than p->ndev, the remaining all-zero
entries are applied and tas2781_cali_preproc() divides by zero on

Accept CRC-less V1 data only if every expected entry is non-zero and
self-consistent (R0 * 1/R0 close to 1.0), otherwise reject it as

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: line6: Reject capture buffers smaller than two packets

line6_capture_copy() splits the copy into the ALSA ring buffer once at
the buffer end and wraps pos_done once, which is only correct when one
packet holds at most buffer_size frames. The packet size comes from the
device's endpoint, and the per-device hw structs allow 64-byte periods
with periods_min 1, so a packet can be larger than the whole buffer.
audio_in_callback() logs an oversized packet and then copies it anyway.

The packet size is known at probe time, so constrain
SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_BYTES in snd_line6_capture_open() to at least
twice the larger of the two endpoints' packet sizes. Two rather than
one, because pos_done advances by the packet and wraps once, so a buffer
of exactly one packet leaves the position unchanged after every packet.
hw_params then rejects a buffer that cannot hold two packets, and the
single wrap is valid for every configuration that gets through. Keep a
guard in line6_capture_copy() that drops an oversized packet with a
ratelimited error, for the case that should no longer be reachable.

Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the GuitarPort
interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 128-byte buffer: ALSA
logged "invalid position: pos = 224, buffer size = 32" and the driver
logged "driver bug: len" on every following packet. With this patch a
1024-byte buffer is refused at hw_params, and a 2048-byte buffer streams
for 30 s with no report and with the position moving inside the buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: caiaq: free the EP4 URB when input setup fails

The three controllers that use the EP4 input URB allocate it before
checking the endpoint type and before registering the input device. On
failure they jump to exit_free_idev, which clears cdev->input_dev but
leaves cdev->ep4_in_urb set. The card teardown then calls
snd_usb_caiaq_input_free(), which returns early because input_dev is
NULL, so the URB is never freed.

Release the URB before dropping the input device on the error path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: usx2y: Require a buffer of two URBs

usx2y_urb_capt_retire() wraps the ring buffer once per packet and
usx2y_urb_play_prepare() once per URB of nr_of_packs() packets of up to
50 frames. Both assume that the data fits in the buffer, and the hw
constraints only require about two 1 ms periods, so a packet larger
than the buffer on capture, or a URB larger than the buffer on playback,
violates that assumption.

Constrain SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_SIZE in snd_usx2y_pcm_open() to at
least two URBs, 2 * nr_of_packs() * 50 frames, for both directions. The
bound is in frames and derived from the driver's own packet limit, so it
does not read the endpoint, whose altsetting is only selected in
prepare. Two URBs rather than one, because the position advances by a
URB on playback and only moves when a URB is less than the whole buffer.
Keep a guard in usx2y_urb_capt_retire() that drops a packet larger than
the buffer, for the case the constraint makes unreachable.

With nrpacks above about 163 (S16_LE) or 109 (S24_3LE) the bound exceeds
the 64 KiB buffer the substream preallocates (twice that with the
preallocation raised to its 128 KiB maximum), so hw_params fails for
those module settings. That is intended: the driver cannot be safe with
a URB larger than half the largest buffer.

Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the US-122
interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 512-byte capture buffer:

  BUG: KASAN: out-of-bounds in i_usx2y_urb_complete+0x1285/0x1ac0
  Read of size 18446744073709551104 at addr ffff88800e448800 by task vhci_rx/83

Tested on 7.3-rc7 with the same device, S16_LE at 44100 Hz, nrpacks 4,
so the bound is 400 frames. A 128-frame capture buffer and a 200-frame
playback buffer are refused at hw_params with EINVAL. A 400-frame buffer
streams for 30 s in each direction with the position advancing inside
the buffer and no KASAN report; the capture guard did not fire. The
same 400-frame capture buffer with S24_3LE, which selects altsetting 2
in prepare, streams for 30 s with the same result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: usx2y: Guard the playback copy

usx2y_urb_play_prepare() sums the packet lengths of a whole URB, copies
that many frames with a single wrap, and sizes each playback packet from
the capture packet's actual_length. Three things are unchecked: that the
URB fits in the ring buffer, that a packet fits in the playback
endpoint's maxpacksize, from which tmpbuf is allocated, and that
actual_length is a whole number of frames. The ISO descriptors take the
raw actual_length while transfer_buffer_length and the copies take
count * stride, so a packet that is not a multiple of the stride makes
the descriptors add up to more than the buffer, by up to stride - 1
bytes per packet.

Return -EPIPE, as the existing packet-size check does, when the URB is
larger than the buffer or a packet is larger than maxpacksize, and size
each descriptor from whole frames, so the descriptors add up to
transfer_buffer_length and each stays within maxpacksize. The buffer
case is prevented by the previous patch and this is the guard for it;
the other two depend only on the device.

The first case is reachable on the unpatched driver with ordinary
packets: on 7.3-rc7, a USB/IP device presenting the US-122 interface
layout and sending 48-frame packets, with a 100-frame playback buffer
(two 50-frame periods, inside the stock constraints), KASAN reports:

  BUG: KASAN: out-of-bounds in i_usx2y_urb_complete+0x79b/0x1ac0
  Read of size 18446744073709551280 at addr ffff88800e6b02e0 by task vhci_rx/80

With both patches, the same device and a 200-frame playback buffer is
refused at hw_params with EINVAL, and a 400-frame buffer plays for 30 s
with the position advancing inside the buffer, no KASAN report and
neither guard message. The maxpacksize check is not exercised: the
emulated device reports the same wMaxPacketSize on both endpoints.

The descriptor case is visible with capture packets of 195 bytes at
stride 4 (48 frames and 3 bytes): without this change the four
descriptors add up to 780 bytes for 768 bytes of data, and USB/IP's
completion check refuses the URB ("total length of iso packets 780 not
equal to actual length of buffer 768", -EPROTO), after which the driver
stops the streams. With this patch every descriptor is 192 bytes, the
descriptors add up to the data in every URB for 30 s, the position
advances inside the buffer and KASAN reports nothing. The 48-frame
playback run above is unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ext2: preserve IOMAP_F_DIRTY for extending direct writes

ext2_iomap_begin() sets IOMAP_F_DIRTY for writes that may extend i_size,
but clears the flag after ext2_get_blocks(). When the write uses an
existing mapped block, iomap can then use FUA and skip
generic_write_sync(), even though ext2_dio_write_end_io() updates the
inode size. An O_DSYNC write can therefore return without persisting
the new size.

For example, on a FUA-capable device, a 512-byte O_DIRECT|O_DSYNC write
at offset 512 into a fsynced one-byte file returns successfully and
extends the in-memory size to 1024, while an immediate read of the
on-disk inode still shows size 1. An explicit fsync persists the new
size.

Move setting of IOMAP_F_DIRTY after the initialization.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/smc: don't spin in smc_rx_recvmsg() while a pipe holds spliced data

While bytes spliced off the RMB are still in a pipe, recvmsg() waits
for the pipe to release them before it copies the data behind them.
The path to that wait skips the timeout and signal checks, and
smc_rx_wait() returns at once on RCV_SHUTDOWN. With a signal pending,
after SHUT_RD, or once the peer closes or shuts down writing,
recvmsg() spins on a CPU until the pipe is drained, and SIGKILL cannot
stop it. MSG_DONTWAIT and an expired SO_RCVTIMEO wait there too
instead of returning -EAGAIN.

Check the timeout and signals before that wait, and end it when the
pipe releases the data or the connection is killed, not on RCV_SHUTDOWN.
A zero-length read returns 0 without waiting for the pipe; a
non-blocking one returns -EAGAIN while poll() still reports the socket
readable (splice() can still take those bytes). The wait sets
SOCKWQ_ASYNC_WAITDATA like smc_rx_wait(), so a byte arriving behind
the pipe raises no SIGIO on a reader already asleep for it, and a full
barrier orders its wait queue entry before its read of splice_pending,
so no wake is lost.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/etnaviv: Fix NULL dereference on unbind without PPU flop reset

flop_reset_data_ppu is only allocated on GPUs that need the PPU flop
reset. However, etnaviv_unbind(..) frees it unconditionally, and
etnaviv_cmdbuf_free(..) dereferences cmdbuf->suballoc before checking
whether cmdbuf is NULL.

As a result, unloading the driver on GPUs that do not need the PPU
flop reset causes a NULL pointer dereference at address 0.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/etnaviv: Flush the tile status cache through both the PE and BLT

Since commit f232d9ec029c ("drm/etnaviv: fix TS cache flushing on GPUs
with BLT engine"), jobs on GPUs with a BLT engine use a BLT command to
flush the tile status cache instead of TS_FLUSH_CACHE, which is broken
on most of these GPUs.

GC7000 r6008/r6009 and GC8200 r6401 are the other way around:
TS_FLUSH_CACHE works, but the BLT command does not flush the cache.
The vendor driver handles these GPUs using TS_FLUSH_CACHE, but the
etnaviv kernel driver has no way to identify them.

As a result, dirty tile status cache lines survive the end of a job.
They are written back by the next cache flush, using the page table of
the job issuing it. If that job belongs to another process, the write
goes to the wrong address space.

On GC7000 r6009 this causes MMU faults and GPU recoveries blamed on an
innocent process. I see around 1100 per run of a multisample
depth/stencil test running alongside two other GPU clients.

Emit both flushes at the end of every job on GPUs with a BLT engine.
Whichever does not work on a given GPU is a no-op. Since dirty lines
are only written back once, this costs one additional state load per
job.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners

mptcp_pm_nl_create_listen_socket() starts the TCP listener directly
instead of going through mptcp_listen(). It consequently misses setting
SOCK_RCU_FREE on the parent MPTCP socket.

tcp_child_process() can invoke the listener's subflow_data_ready()
callback without holding the MPTCP parent lock or a reference to the
parent. An authenticated MP_JOIN racing with endpoint teardown can
therefore access the parent after its last reference has been dropped.
The ADD_ADDR error path can also close an already published listener.

Set SOCK_RCU_FREE before __inet_listen_sk() publishes the TCP listener,
matching mptcp_listen(). This protects the parent on every subsequent
close path, including a failed endpoint addition.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: don't let the extent type hide an exhausted free-space table extent

udf_table_new_block() takes the first block of the free-space table
extent closest to the goal.  It keeps that extent's type and length
together in goal_elen, subtracts one block, and deletes the extent only
if goal_elen then reaches zero.  UDF 2.60 section 2.3.7.1 requires the
free-space extents of an Unallocated Space Entry to be of type 1
(allocated but not recorded), and mkudffs writes them that way.  For
such an extent the type bits keep goal_elen non-zero, so taking its last
block leaves a type-1 extent of length zero behind, starting at the
block after the extent, which is in use.

The next allocation that picks this empty extent returns that in-use
block.  Subtracting a block from 0x40000000 then borrows from the type
bits, and the extent becomes type 0 with a length of 2^30 - blocksize:
about a gigabyte of "free" space overlapping live metadata, the other
table extents and whatever lies behind the partition.  From then on
blocks are handed out twice, or past the end of the partition.

Extents that udf_table_free_blocks() adds are type 0, where the check
works, so only tables written by mkudffs or by another implementation
are affected.  Nothing more than filling such a filesystem is needed:
on a fresh 1 MiB "mkudffs --space=unalloctable" image, creating empty
files until the partition is full writes file entries over the reserve
volume descriptor sequence and the backup anchor, and df then reports a
negative amount of used space.

On syzbot's images the same double allocation is what the two reports
below trip over.  In the first, ftruncate() extends a new file with
enough hole extents to need a chain of allocation extent descriptors;
one AED is placed on another inode's file entry, and a later one is
placed on the block of the AED currently being filled, which
udf_setup_indirect_aext() zeroes, so __udf_add_aext() finds
lengthAllocDescs out of step with its cursor.  In the second, an AED
is placed past the end of the device, sb_getblk() fails, and the error
path of udf_do_extend_file() calls udf_truncate_extents() on an extent
list that no longer covers i_size.

Keep the type separately from the length, as udf_table_prealloc_blocks()
already does.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: check the unallocated space table when it is loaded

udf_table_new_block() hands out the first block of the extent closest
to its goal and trusts that the extent covers at least one whole block
inside the partition.  Nothing checks that.  A zero-length extent makes
it return the block the extent points at, which need not be free, and
the subtraction of one block then underflows the length into the type
bits, turning the entry into a bogus continuation.  An extent running
past the end of the partition makes it return blocks behind the
partition.

Such tables are not only found on crafted images: until the previous
commit, udf_table_new_block() itself left zero-length extents behind
in tables written by mkudffs, and then converted them into extents
running past the partition.

Check every extent once when the table is loaded, and refuse
read-write access if one is empty, is not a whole number of blocks, or
does not lie inside the partition, in the same way as for other
allocation information the kernel cannot use.  Check first that the
table is an Unallocated Space Entry at all: the walk starts at the
offset of the allocation descriptors in one, and for a file entry that
offset lies before the inode's in-memory copy of the descriptors.
Treat a chain of allocation extent descriptors that leads back to
itself the same way: the walk would otherwise return the same extents
forever, and the mount would never finish.  Let a fatal signal
interrupt the walk and fail the mount.

Refusing read-write access to an empty extent is deliberate.  It shows
that an old kernel took the last block but left the entry behind.  If
consumed again, the entry returns an in-use block and turns into a huge
bogus extent.  Refusing the table before that
happens avoids this second allocation; the filesystem can still be
mounted read-only.  The check cannot detect every overlap that may
already exist in a damaged table.

This patch should be backported together with the previous one: that
patch stops creating new empty extents, and this one rejects existing
ones before they are consumed again.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: fix preallocation discarding before an empty allocation extent

udf_discard_prealloc() finds the last extent of a file by peeking at
the next one with udf_next_aext() and stopping when that returns 0.
The peek reads into eloc and elen, and the code then uses them as the
last extent.  But when udf_next_aext() returns 0 they hold no defined
value: if the extent list ends in a continuation descriptor that leads
to an empty allocation extent, they describe that continuation, i.e.
the block of the empty allocation extent, one block long.

The kernel creates such lists itself: when udf_delete_aext() removes
the only descriptor of the last allocation extent in a list, it leaves
that allocation extent empty and the continuation to it in place.

If the last extent is a preallocation, udf_discard_prealloc() deletes
it with udf_delete_aext(), which finds the following allocation extent
empty, so it also removes the continuation and frees that allocation
extent's block.  udf_discard_prealloc() then frees eloc and elen: that
block a second time, instead of the preallocated blocks.  On a space
bitmap the preallocated blocks leak and the free block count drifts.
On an unallocated space table the second free adds a second free
extent for the same block, which is later handed out twice: fsx as run
by generic/091 and generic/263 ends up with two parts of its test file
in one block and reads back bad data.

Peek into separate variables, so that eloc and elen keep the last
extent that udf_next_aext() returned with 1.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: don't use eloc after the end of the unallocated space table

When udf_next_aext() returns 0, its eloc, elen and etype outputs hold
no defined value.  Two walks of the unallocated space table still use
eloc after the walk has reached the end of the table.

udf_table_prealloc_blocks() looks for a free extent starting at
first_block and decides whether it found one by comparing eloc with
first_block after the walk.  If the table's list ends in a continuation
descriptor that leads to an empty allocation extent, eloc is then the
block of that allocation extent, which is in use, and if that is
first_block, the block is handed out as preallocation.  Once
udf_discard_prealloc() no longer frees the wrong block, this is what
still makes fsx in generic/091 and generic/263 read back bad data on a
table, in about one run in four.  Only take the extent if the walk
stopped at it.

When udf_table_free_blocks() cannot merge the freed blocks into an
existing extent, it appends a new one and sets only its block number,
so the partition reference comes from whatever eloc held after the
walk, and with long allocation descriptors it is written to disk.  For
a table without extents, eloc was never set.  Take the partition
reference from the freed blocks instead.  Short allocation descriptors
do not store the partition reference, which is why this half remains a
latent long-descriptor fix rather than a reproduced failure.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

MIPS: sgi-ip32: Leave MACE PCI control alone in config accesses

mace_pci_read_config() clears the master abort interrupt enable in the
MACE PCI control register around each config read. A register read
followed by two register writes can hang CRIME 1.1 under DMA load.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu()

list_splice_init_rcu() makes a list look empty to new readers, waits for
the current ones with the given sync function, and only then links the
entries into the new list. The sync function takes no argument, so it
can wait for RCU readers but not for the readers of an srcu_struct.

Passing synchronize_rcu() for a list read under SRCU still builds, but
leaves SRCU readers on the entries while the last one's next pointer is
moved onto the new list head. nvme_remove_namespaces() does this today.

Add list_splice_init_srcu(), which waits for the readers of the given
srcu_struct instead.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme: wait for SRCU readers before splicing the namespace list

Readers walk ctrl->namespaces under ctrl->srcu, and some of them sleep
there, e.g. nvme_wait_freeze() waiting for I/O to drain.

nvme_remove_namespaces() moves the list onto its on-stack ns_list with
list_splice_init_rcu(), which only waits for RCU readers before
relinking the entries. A reader still on the last namespace then follows
its next pointer to ns_list instead of ctrl->namespaces and treats the
stack as a namespace. Deleting a controller while a Format NVM
passthrough waits for a delayed read on the last namespace gives:

  BUG: KASAN: stack-out-of-bounds in nvme_wait_freeze+0x102/0x120
  Read of size 8 at addr ff110001d2f3fc38 by task nvme/4413
  Call Trace:
   nvme_wait_freeze
   nvme_passthru_start
   nvme_submit_user_cmd
   nvme_user_cmd
   nvme_dev_ioctl
  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff8af04850

Use list_splice_init_srcu() instead, which waits for the SRCU readers.
This also takes the RCU grace period out of every controller deletion.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched/fair: Clear throttle state when leaving the fair class

Task-based CFS bandwidth throttling removes a task's fair sched_entity
while the scheduler core still considers the task queued. p->throttled
carries the fair-specific state across dequeue/enqueue operations.

DEQUEUE_CLASS removes the task from cfs_rq->throttled_limbo_list
but retains the bit. If the last finite CFS quota is disabled while
the task runs in another class, it is absent from the unthrottle walk and
the bit survives.
Returning to fair while cfs_bandwidth_used() is false then performs a real
fair enqueue with p->throttled still set.

After bandwidth is re-enabled, a class-change dequeue treats the
stale bit as limbo state and skips __dequeue_task(). p->se.on_rq therefore
remains set, and put_prev_task_fair() places the entity in the EEVDF tree
while the task moves to RT. On exit, the fair picker can select the
TASK_DEAD task. __schedule() then returns to do_task_dead(),
which hits BUG().

Keep p->throttled across migrations and group moves, but clear it on
DEQUEUE_CLASS because fair-specific state must not outlive fair-class
membership. A later return to fair uses the normal enqueue path. That path
still respects a throttled cfs_rq.

A KASAN, LOCKDEP and DEBUG_LIST v7.3 kernel reproduced the do_task_dead()
BUG in 3/3 root and 3/3 delegated uid-1000 runs with CapPrm=CapEff=0 and
RLIMIT_RTPRIO=1. The fix passed both matrices plus a 3/3 class-switch
control with bandwidth continuously enabled, without a scheduler warning,
KASAN report, lockdep splat or crash.

An AI coding assistant analyzed the state mismatch and drafted the initial
reproducer, fix candidate and this changelog. The source paths, trigger,
controls and results were rechecked against the cited revisions.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

arm64: sdei: Preserve the interrupted context's exception registers

An SDEI event is dispatched by firmware regardless of PSTATE.DAIF, so it
can interrupt the kernel where the exception registers are live:

 - exception entry, before kernel_entry has saved ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and
   before the C handler has read ESR_EL1/FAR_EL1;
 - exception return, after kernel_exit has loaded ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and
   before the ERET.

An IRQ or pseudo-NMI cannot arrive there with PSTATE.I set. Firmware
saves only x0-x17, PC and PSTATE around an SDEI event, so a synchronous
exception taken by the handler overwrites the interrupted context's
ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR. do_sdei_event() only notices that ELR changed,
and warns.

The interrupted context then carries on with the handler's state. A
task interrupted on its way into the kernel can be sent SIGILL for the
handler's kernel data abort. A task interrupted on its way back to user
space ERETs to EL1, at the handler's fixup address, with user registers
loaded.

With SDEI delivering NMI backtraces, this happens in normal operation.
The handler runs show_regs(), which reads through possibly-NULL pointers
with the _nofault() accessors. print_worker_info() faults this way for a
kworker that is not running a work item, and a single sysrq-l warned
once per such kworker.

Save ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR in __sdei_handler() before
irqentry_nmi_enter(), which can take an exception too, and restore them
after irqentry_nmi_exit().

Once they are restored, a nested exception is harmless if its handler is
safe in NMI context. That holds for EL1 data aborts on translation,
permission and access-flag faults, which never take the mmap lock in NMI
context, and for BRK. Warn once, with the syndrome, about any other
exception class.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes

On AMD CPUs with INVLPGB, two live processes can get the same MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE
global ASID value. The two then hit each other's TLB entries, so each can read
or corrupt the other's memory.

The global ASID space is managed lazily. When a global ASID is freed, its bit is
set in the global_asid_freed bitmap. Once the free ASID search reaches the end
of the global_asid_used bitmap, a global flush is done to really reclaim the
lazily freed global ASIDs.

However, the current code can assign the same global ASID to two different
processes, if one process is assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE - 1, another process
MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, and both stick around (keeping their global ASID numbers in
use) until the search wraps around again.  At that point a third process could
also get assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE.

    the highest ASID stays in use, so it is not handed out again
      last_global_asid stays below it, so no reset
        the clear bits run out
          find_next_zero_bit() returns MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE
            global_asid_available > 0, so the failure is not caught
              MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE is handed out as an ASID

A search only looks at the bits below MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, so it cannot see that
this value is in use. The next failed search hands it out again, even if the
first process still holds it.

The fix used here is to reset the global ASID space after a failed search, and
to search again. If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out.

The test for !global_asid_available is removed, because use_global_asid() only
calls allocate_global_asid() if global_asid_available > 0. The remaining test is
for a condition that should be impossible.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size

IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE)
that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table.
For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the
IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the
device table.

The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB
pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the
out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit
this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring
down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device
table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB.

Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected
processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a
(Zen5/BRH).

This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963.

kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size
encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches
pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched
kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB,
so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs
that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this
patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel
and the crash kernel together.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data()

The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the
client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need()
only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes.
ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio
with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more
inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end.

Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant()
and fill_inode(), are covered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client

When a ROAMING_ADV is received for an announced local client,
batadv_tt_local_mark_removed() sets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM, queues a
DEL|ROAM change and marks the entry as BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING. If the
client sends a frame again before the next TTVN commit,
batadv_tt_local_add_existing() only clears the PENDING flag and returns
early. The ADD cancels the queued DEL, but the entry keeps the ROAM flag:

* batadv_is_my_client() reports the client as not served by this node
* batadv_tt_local_client_is_roaming() reroutes unicast frames for it to
  the node which sent the ROAMING_ADV

The ROAM flag is only removed with the next frame of the client.

Since BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM is set together with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING,
it has to be cleared also at the same time with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING
when the client roamed back.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events

In the first implementation of the translation table events, it was only
possible to announce:

* ADD: new locally detected client
* DEL: disappeared local client

If an ADD event was queued and then a DEL event was queued in the same
timeslot, it is valid to destroy both events because nothing actually
changed for remode nodes

But with commit 3c4f7ab60cc2 ("batman-adv: improve the TT component to
support runtime flag changes") and subsequent changes, it could also happen
that there are extra ADD events:

* ADD: _NEW_ locally detected client
* ADD: already existing client with new flags
* DEL: disappeared local client

The first and the last type of event could in theory still be removed
together from the (to be announced) events queue. But if the "update flags"
ADD is dropped together with the DEL, it would still leave global
translation table of a remote node in the incorrect state - believing that
the client didn't disappear.

If a detected client was previously announced, a DEL event must only
overwrite the "update flags" ADD but the DEL itself must still continue to
exist in the (to be anounced) events queue. For now, adjustment of the
announced flags is used for everything instead of dropping already queued
up events completely.

Similarly, a DEL followed by an ADD caused both entries to be deleted. But
the new ADD could announce flags changes which were not yet present for the
client before it was marked for DELetion. The new ADD must therefore only
overwrite the DEL - but still be kept.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ata: libata-scsi: reject data-in commands with a data-out buffer

SG_IO can submit a data-in SCSI command with DMA_TO_DEVICE. The
scatterlist can then contain pages pinned without write access.
ata_scsi_rbuf_fill() writes simulated replies to that scatterlist;
in the reported case, the copy tried to write the shared zero page
and faulted in the kernel.

The same mismatch can affect SG_IO commands translated by libata.
ZBC IN and GET PHYSICAL ELEMENT STATUS completion handlers can modify
the receive buffer even if the drive aborts the command. For ATAPI,
the successful INQUIRY completion also rewrites the buffer in
atapi_fixup_inquiry().

Reject these mismatched commands before the buffer is written or the
command is issued. Report ABORTED COMMAND / DATA IN BUFFER ERROR because
the CDB itself can be valid; the supplied transfer direction is wrong.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA

The erratum (MMU-700: #3777127, S3: #3673557) deals with under
invalidation of a CONT PTE grouping in the SMMU. The recommended work
around is to use a range invalidation that spans the entire CONT. The only
user of CONT in the kernel right now is through SVA sharing a CPU page
table that contains a CONT created by the mm.

Previously it was thought that this errata was dealt with because the
driver always uses range invalidation. However, there is a subtle detail
in the errata that the invalidation range must fully enclose the entire
CONT for it to work.

It seems that two sequential range invalidations, with a split point
falling inside a CONT grouping, will not prevent the errata.

The SMMU's range invalidation generation algorithm does not produce a
single invalidation for a single SVA invalidation request, nor does the mm
carefully align the SVA invalidation ranges to accommodate the splitting
of the invalidation into several ranges.

Thus, when processing a SVA invalidation, the range invalidation splitting
routine can generate a range invalidation that is split in the middle of
the CONT and risk under invalidation from this errata. This condition
could be triggered by a malicious userspace manipulating the TLB gathers
via mmap/mprotect/munmap.

Update the errata list to the include the S3 variation, detect the IOMMUs
that have it, and then have SVA invalidations use a simplified version of
the over invalidation algorithm from the tlbi rework series. This ensures
that a single range invalidation is issued for a single MMU notifier
callback and now the range invalidation is guarenteed to cover any posible
CONT.

Future work to add CONT to iommu_domain page tables should either use this
one-invalidate/one-range invalidation algorithm or disable CONT support in
the iommu_domain.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort()

gmem_abort() maps at s2fd->fault_ipa, which HPFAR_EL2 holds at 4K
granularity whatever the page size. The generic page-table code aligns
it, but pkvm_pgtable_stage2_map() looks up existing mappings over
[addr, addr + size), so on a pKVM host with pages larger than 4K a
guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can
find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault
forever.

The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested
guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one
kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on.

Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as
user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault
exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd
memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: hold shkey across socket migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the
new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops
the skb-owned shared-key reference.

If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the
final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the
freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference.

Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release
it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected
authentication key throughout the ownership transfer.

Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and
validated by Trail of Bits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained
control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can
therefore access the socket after it has been freed.

Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use
sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA
ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it
is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers.

Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration
so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings

find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that
are not CoW mappings, which is wrong.

If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have
VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE.

While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires
VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon()
still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma.

This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such
that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that
actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would
require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first
place.

copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared
PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are
shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function
with shareable page tables is the real issue.

If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it
might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant
locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and
possibly freed after calling:

	dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz);

To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a
safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never
end up messing with shared PMD tables in there.

Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd
operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an
anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma.

As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and
also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well
directly for consistency.

A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma)
lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of
VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on
CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery

In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to
TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is
asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so
frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's
mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside
the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of
1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues
behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds
after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore,
and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll
("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The
AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and
only a reboot recovers.

mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets
IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one
station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing
unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with
the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1
("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else
leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the
usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets
the backlog build up.

On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven
through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU
and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with
it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue

Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons
only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool.
The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one
station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the
drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single
client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page
count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there
for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit
queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for
anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon
valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers.

Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the
measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on
the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its
access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded
by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at
the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone

In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds
any underlying queue limits:
1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This
   limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and
   device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS
   writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges
   contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without
   checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM
   target enforces a smaller limit.
2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment
   limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the
   128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages
   are discontiguous.
3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs,
   section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never
   spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors.

Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split()
submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head
half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail
bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head:

  dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048
  != wp_offset 248, len 248

The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing
f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only:
